title: The lakes we are not draining
content: South Lhonak lake had pipes in it. For years, engineers had run siphons over its moraine wall to drain the water down and buy the valley a little safety. On the night of 3 October 2023, none of it mattered. A slab of frozen mountainside, about 14.7 million cubic metres of rock and ice, broke off and crashed into the lake. The water heaved back a wave some 20 metres high, tore through the loose wall of debris that had held it for decades, and sent roughly 50 million cubic metres down the Teesta. By the time the surge reached Chungthang, 60 km below, it was deep enough to swallow the 1,200 MW Teesta-III dam, the largest in Sikkim. It did not stop there. The flood was tracked for hundreds of kilometres down the river, through Singtam and Rangpo and on towards Bangladesh. At least 55 people were killed, scores more were never found, and around 80,000 were hit across four districts. We have since reconstructed that night almost minute by minute, in a study led by Ashim Sattar of IIT Bhubaneswar and published in Science in January 2025. The harder thing to explain is that we did not need to wait for it. South Lhonak had sat on every glaciologist’s watch-list for years. It had been studied, modelled, even fitted with siphons to lower it. Its swelling was visible from space. The disaster was not unforeseeable. It was unforewarned. That gap, between what we can see and what we actually act on, is the real Himalayan hazard of this decade. A glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF, is one of the few catastrophes that announces itself in slow motion. As a glacier retreats, meltwater gathers behind the rubble the ice leaves, a natural dam often no stronger than a heap of gravel. The lake behind it grows, season upon season, until something, a rockfall, a heatwave, an avalanche into the water, tips it over. The trigger comes without warning. The loaded gun, however, sits in plain sight, filling visibly, often for a generation.

title: Extreme heat-related pregnancy complications rising, putting pregnant women, new-borns at risk
content: Extreme heat is already increasing health risks for pregnant women and new-borns, with nearly three-quarters of maternal healthcare professionals across five countries reporting a rise in heat-related cases and complications over the past five years, according to a new international survey. The survey, commissioned by global health foundation Wellcome, covered 1,000 healthcare professionals in India, Australia, Brazil, the United Kingdom and Zimbabwe. Around 73 per cent of maternal healthcare respondents said they had seen an increase in heat-related cases or complications affecting pregnant women, while 76 per cent reported an increase in cases affecting foetal or new-born health. Nearly all those surveyed said they had personally cared for a pregnant woman or baby whose health they believed had been adversely affected by extreme heat. This included 98 per cent who had treated pregnant women and 99 per cent who had cared for babies. The findings were released on October 5, 2026, first day of the official pre-COP ministerial meeting in Fiji, ahead of the 31st Conference of Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), scheduled for November 9-20. The survey was conducted online between September 17 and October 1, 2026, with 200 maternal healthcare professionals surveyed in each of the five countries. The findings come at a time when 33 countries this recorded their hottest July, underscoring the growing threat extreme heat poses to health systems and communities worldwide. The survey also comes amid growing scientific evidence linking heat exposure during pregnancy with adverse outcomes including preterm birth, low birth weight, stillbirth and maternal complications. Research cited by Wellcome found that for every 1 degree Celsius rise in heat exposure, the odds of preterm birth increase by around 5 per cent, while exposure to heatwaves was associated with a 25 per cent higher risk of obstetric complications. Healthcare professionals surveyed by Wellcome also reported seeing specific problems they associated with extreme heat. Around 23 per cent said they had encountered pregnancy complications requiring additional monitoring or treatment, while 34 per cent reported cases of low birth weight or restricted growth. Another 36 per cent said they had seen dehydration and heat-related illness among new-borns, while 33 per cent reported difficulties involving feeding, breathing and temperature regulation. Extreme heat was also affecting access to healthcare. More than a quarter of respondents, or 27 per cent, said high temperatures were making it harder for pregnant women and families to travel to or access care, while 29 per cent reported an increase in urgent or emergency presentations. But even more worrying was that healthcare workers expect the problem to worsen. Around 81 per cent of those surveyed said they were concerned that extreme heat would pose a growing threat to maternal, foetal and new-born health over the next five years unless further action was taken. “Extreme heat, fuelled by climate change is impacting our way of life and our health — and yet many countries are not prepared. With El Niño pushing temperatures higher, the failure to act is costing lives,” said Madeleine Thomson, head of climate impacts and adaptation at Wellcome. She added that measures such as early warning systems and cooler buildings were already available but often failed to reach those most at risk. Meanwhile, UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell, speaking at an event on maternal health and global heating on October 5, described pregnancy and birth as an emerging “faultline” in the climate crisis. “The picture is clear and very disturbing: as extreme heat worsens, pregnancy and birth are now a new faultline in the global climate crisis, and one which is potentially fatal,” Stiell said. He warned that the risks would fall disproportionately on those already facing limited access to healthcare, safe housing, cooling, water and electricity. “‘Staying cool’ is simply not an option when there is no cool place to go,” he said. Ahead of COP31, Wellcome is calling for pregnant women, new mothers and babies to be explicitly included in national climate and health plans, with funded and accountable measures to protect them from heat. It has also called for the development of the first World Health Organization clinical guidance on heat, pregnancy and the postpartum period, as well as stronger data and surveillance systems that integrate heat exposure into maternal and new-born health monitoring.

title: Favourable weather gives Kashmir’s paddy farmers their best harvest in years
content: Around 25 kilometres south of Srinagar, in the Kakapora area of Pulwama district, farmers are cutting paddy with a sense of relief they have not felt for a long time. After years of floods, dry spells and uneven weather, this season has brought the temperature, sunshine and rainfall that rice needs to grow well. Harvesting has begun in several parts of Kashmir, including Kulgam, Anantnag, Pulwama and Ganderbal. Cultivators say the crop is better than in recent seasons, and many hope it will improve their incomes after repeated losses. Mohammad Maqbool Ganaie, 47, a farmer from Wandakhpora village, said he thanked God for a harvest he had not seen in 15 years. He said farmers had faced water shortages for many years, but this year the rains were sufficient. He also recalled how badly last year went. “Last year, floods destroyed our crops as water submerged the paddy fields. It remained there till harvesting season,” he said. Abdul Rasheed, 70, from the Awantipora area, described a similar change. He said the yield this year was surprisingly higher than in previous years. His fields have long suffered because the river is far away and the water level is often too low to reach the lift irrigation pumps. This year, he said, continuous rain solved that problem and brought a better yield after many years. Waheed Ur Rehman, Chief Agriculture Officer of Pulwama, said temperatures stayed in line with what the paddy crop requires. He also credited new high density varieties from the Shalimar Rice (SR) series for the good production. He cautioned that exact figures are not yet available because harvesting is still under way. He said that in areas like Pulwama, varieties such as SR 4, SR 2 and Shalimar Sugandh-1 (SS-1) are widely grown, along with K 332, a high altitude variety released in 1982. According to him, these varieties resist diseases such as rice blast better. He added that farmers are also becoming more aware of zinc deficiency in their soil. Crop Cut Experiments are under way to measure this year’s output, and the official said exact figures will follow once the harvest ends. “For now we estimate a far better production this year compared to previous years,” he said. Weather data supports what farmers describe. According to the India Meteorological Department, Jammu and Kashmir received 259.7 mm of rainfall in July, against a normal of 192.6 mm. That is a surplus of 35 per cent, and it followed a long period of below normal rainfall. Most districts in the Kashmir Valley received more rain than usual. Baramulla recorded the highest surplus at 165 per cent, followed by Ganderbal at 110 per cent and Pulwama at 108 per cent. Srinagar and Anantnag each recorded a surplus of 71 per cent. Kulgam, Bandipora, Kupwara and Budgam recorded surpluses of 51, 33, 32 and six per cent respectively. Shopian was the only Valley district with a deficit, at 40 per cent. Mohammad Anees, an environmentalist based in Kashmir, said temperature and rainfall conditions appear to have suited paddy in South Kashmir. Moisture was available during the key stages of crop growth, and the crop did not face long periods of water stress. He noted that last year’s rainfall was erratic and excessive, while this year’s was better spread across the season. He also warned that growing climate variability remains a concern for future farming. The contrast with last year is sharp. In September, days of heavy rain submerged thousands of hectares across Jammu and Kashmir, damaging paddy fields and apple orchards. Rivers and streams flowed above the danger mark and flooded low lying farmland. Farmers said the water flattened standing paddy, washed away fertile soil and swept away orchards along with their trees. When harvest time arrived, many fields were still under water. Farmers could not cut their crop, and some were forced to burn the standing paddy instead. For families who depend on rice for both food and income, it was a heavy blow. A study by SKUAST Kashmir in 2020 found that paddy is grown on about 1.5 lakh (0.15 million) hectares in the Valley. In Pulwama district alone, 16,500 hectares are under paddy. Even so, the long term trend gives cause for concern. The area under paddy in the Kashmir Division has fallen from approximately 1.69 lakh (0.169 million) hectares in 1980 to nearly 1.29 lakh (0.129 million) hectares in 2024. That is a reduction of about 40,000 hectares, or nearly 24 per cent. The area rose briefly to around 1.36 lakh (0.136 million) hectares in 2017, but it declined again in the years that followed. This suggests that the loss of paddy land is not a short term change. It points to a continuing shift in how farmland is used. Better crop productivity has offset part of the decline, but it does not remove the worry. If paddy acreage keeps falling, a good harvest in one year cannot by itself secure the future of rice farming in the Valley. For now, farmers in Kakapora, Awantipora and nearby villages are focused on bringing in the crop. Many say this season has restored some of their confidence. Officials say the final numbers will show how large the gain really is, and the Crop Cut Experiments will provide those figures once harvesting ends. The season has shown how closely Kashmir’s rice farmers depend on the weather. A year of balanced rain and suitable temperatures has delivered a good yield, while a year of floods brought ruin. As the climate becomes less predictable, supporting resistant varieties, protecting paddy land and improving water access will matter as much as a good monsoon.

title: Daily weather tracker: Monsoon retreat brings rain and thunderstorms to North India, heavy showers in south
content: Summary Monsoon retreat: North India braces for thunderstorms, gusty winds and rain, while southern states face heavy showers and weather warnings. Heavy rain alert: Kerala, Tamil Nadu and South Interior Karnataka may receive heavy rainfall as active weather systems influence southern India. Delhi weather: Delhi-NCR could witness sudden thunderstorms, lightning, gusty winds and light rain, although heavy rainfall remains unlikely during this period. Eastern India: Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal may experience thunderstorms, rain and winds reaching 40 kilometres per hour. Temperatures rise: Sri Ganganagar recorded 39.7°C, while Haflong registered 16°C, highlighting contrasting temperatures across different parts of the country.
